name: Priya
definition: Priya is a composite portrait of a young woman supervisor in Mandya's silk-reeling economy, navigating factory pressures, household duties and the schooling hopes she carries for her children in a taluk where cane migration and factory attendance shape family calendars. She embodies the dailiness of work, care and aspiration in the Cauvery belt's towns, where women's labour anchors both silk and sugar economies yet remains underpaid and double-burdened.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Priya supervises a floor of twenty reeling basins at a privately owned silk unit on the Maddur-Malavalli road, checking thread count, basin temperature and worker attendance from seven each morning until four in the afternoon. She earns eleven thousand rupees a month, a step above the nine thousand paid to basin workers but still modest given her responsibility for quality and output targets set by the cocoon trader who owns the unit. The work is hot and humid, her sari edge perpetually damp, her fingers quick to spot a break in the filament. Prices for Ramanagara cocoons have been uneven this year, so her employer delayed the Ugadi bonus and now talks of reducing shifts if orders from Mysuru weavers slacken. She walks twenty minutes each way, leaving home before her children wake and returning in time to help with homework. Evenings she cooks, oversees the older girl's tuition homework, pumps water from the shared borewell tap and manages the grocery budget her husband hands her each week. Inflation in ration-shop items outside the Anna Bhagya quota presses hard; she has stopped buying the better Nandini milk her mother-in-law wants and uses the cheaper pouch brand instead.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Priya lives with her husband, two daughters aged nine and six, her mother-in-law and her husband's younger unmarried brother in a rented two-room house on the edge of Maddur town. Her husband drives a lorry on the Bengaluru-Mysuru route, away three or four nights a week, so the daily rhythm of meals, children's baths and her mother-in-law's diabetes medication falls to her. She was married at nineteen, shortly after failing her second-year PU commerce exams, to a boy from her mother's village; the match was arranged through a relative and her family paid a modest dowry of jewellery and vessels. Her elder daughter is in fourth standard at the government Kannada-medium school two streets away, the younger in first; Priya wants both to finish tenth and go to PU college, something she could not do herself. Her mother-in-law, a widow, helps with morning breakfast but tires easily and spends afternoons watching television; the younger brother-in-law works irregular construction jobs and contributes little to household expenses. Priya's own mother, a farm labourer in a Mandya taluk village, visits occasionally and brings homegrown ragi; Priya sends money when she can. Gender roles are unquestioned in the household: Priya does all cooking and cleaning, her husband controls the earnings and the mother-in-law expects deference, yet Priya has learned to assert small decisions about the girls' schooling and clinic visits.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Priya herself studied in a government Kannada school up to tenth standard in her natal village, then enrolled in a town PU college for commerce but found the English textbooks and commute overwhelming and dropped out after failing second-year exams; marriage followed within months. She regrets not finishing PU and is determined her daughters will. Both girls attend the nearby government primary school where the midday meal is reliable and the Shakti bus pass, though not yet needed, will help when they reach high school age and must travel to the better secondary school near the bus stand. Priya pays three hundred rupees a month for private tuition in mathematics and English for the elder girl, worried that the school's English teaching is weak and that without it her daughter will face the same wall she did. The younger girl is still settling in, often distracted; Priya scolds her to sit still and finish her Kannada alphabet practice each evening. School costs—books, fees, uniforms, the annual sports-day contribution—add up to over three thousand a year for both, manageable but tight. Priya dreams of them studying through PU, perhaps even a BCom in Mandya town or Mysuru, and finding salaried office or bank jobs rather than factory or farm work, though she knows tuition fees rise steeply after tenth and worries whether her husband will agree to the expense for daughters.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Priya's health worries centre on her mother-in-law's diabetes, her own recurring lower-back pain from years of standing at the reeling unit and her younger daughter's repeated coughs. Her mother-in-law's insulin and test strips cost nearly a thousand rupees a month even after the Arogya Karnataka card discount at the government taluk hospital; Priya must remind her to take the evening dose and watches her diet, though the old woman resents being denied sweets. Priya herself has not seen a doctor for her back pain, relying on a balm from the medical shop and occasional painkillers when the ache is sharp; she knows she should rest more but cannot afford to miss work. The younger girl had a chest infection last monsoon that required antibiotics from the private clinic, an expense of fifteen hundred rupees they could not avoid. The anganwadi near their old house provided immunisations when the girls were infants, but now the daughters are beyond that age and Priya must take them to the taluk hospital for any serious illness, waiting two or three hours for an outpatient consultation. Contraception was advised after her second delivery and she took injections for a few years, stopping only when her husband objected; she now relies on the calendar method, anxious about another pregnancy she cannot afford. The reeling-unit air is humid and thread dust makes many workers cough chronically; Priya notices it in herself but dismisses it as unavoidable. She drinks turmeric milk some nights and trusts that youth and care will see the family through.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Priya was born into a Vokkaliga farming family and married into another Vokkaliga household, the marriage arranged within the jati network through relatives who knew both families. Caste shapes social life quietly but firmly: neighbors are mostly Vokkaliga or SC families who work in silk or cane, and her mother-in-law insists the family not share food vessels with the SC neighbour despite Priya's discomfort with the practice. Priya visits the Anjaneya temple near the bus stand every Thursday evening when she finishes work early, lighting a lamp and asking for her children's health and her husband's safe travel on the highway. During Ugadi the family makes holige and Priya takes a half-day to visit her mother's village; the Dasara procession in Mysuru is something she has seen only once, on a school trip years ago, and thinks of as grand but distant. Her mother-in-law observes fasts for Varalakshmi and Karva Chauth and expects Priya to do the same, which she does to keep peace though she finds the daylong hunger hard after a factory shift. Priya has a few friends from the reeling unit, women she chats with during the lunch break and sometimes meets at the market, but little time for organised socialising. Community ties are dense yet uncodified: a neighbour lends rice when the ration runs short before month-end, Priya returns it; her brother-in-law's construction crew includes men from the same caste cluster.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Priya's household receives Anna Bhagya rice and subsidised kerosene through the ration shop, the card in her mother-in-law's name but Priya collects it monthly. The free-bus Shakti scheme has not yet affected her daily walk to the factory, but she knows it will help when her daughters reach high school and must travel farther; her mother-in-law has started using the KSRTC bus to visit relatives in Pandavapura without asking Priya's husband for fare money, a small shift in independence Priya welcomes. The family has an Ayushman Bharat card but has used it only once, for the younger daughter's hospitalisations; Priya finds the empanelled hospitals slow and the staff dismissive of Kannada queries. Priya has heard of the government's scholarship for SC girls but does not know if anything similar exists for OBC or general-category children; no one at the school has mentioned it. Her employer once promised ESI coverage but never enrolled the unit, and she has no written contract or leave policy. She blames the owner for this, not the government, though she knows labour inspectors rarely visit small silk units.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Priya's foremost worry is money: whether her husband's lorry income will stay steady, whether she can keep both daughters in school through tenth, and whether the silk unit will cut shifts if cocoon prices stay weak. She is proud she works and contributes to the household, yet resents that her earnings are not recognised as hers to decide upon; her husband controls even the modest savings she wishes to keep for her daughters' future fees. She blames inflation and the unsteady cocoon market for the family's tightness and believes government help for farmers and workers reaches only those with connections or the right caste certificates. Priya sees education as the only ladder out of factory and farm labour for her daughters and fears that anything—a sudden expense, her husband's refusal, an early marriage proposal from a relative—could derail that chance. She takes quiet satisfaction in supervising twenty workers and ensuring the day's output meets the target, a skill her mother never had, but knows that without further study she will not rise beyond this. Priya is not especially interested in state or national politics, though she listens when neighbors discuss Cauvery releases and water shortages during the summer, and she accepts that richer, English-educated families in Mysuru and Bengaluru get better schools, jobs and hospitals. She asks for her daughters' health, her mother-in-law's manageable decline and her own strength to keep working, modest demands framed as prayers rather than rights, hoping that steadiness and care will inch the family forward despite the pressures that push against them.
